Chapter 2: Building Confidence and a Positive Self-Image
Now that we’ve got the basics down, let’s talk about something that really shapes our journey—confidence.
For a lot of folks with dyslexia, school can be tough. Imagine working so hard on a reading or spelling assignment, only to feel left behind while others seem to breeze through. It’s easy for those moments to chip away at your self-worth.
But here’s the good news—confidence isn’t something you’re either born with or not. It’s something you build, step by step, through small wins and with the support of people who believe in you.
Think about the difference it makes when a parent, teacher, or mentor says, “I know you can do this.” That belief is powerful. It can change everything.
One of the best ways to help someone with dyslexia—whether it’s a child or even yourself—is to celebrate effort, not just results. Let’s say a child spends extra time on a reading assignment. Instead of only praising perfect spelling or how fast they finished, shine a light on their creativity and determination. This simple shift lets them know that what really matters is the effort they put in, and the growth they’re making.
There are some practical strategies that can really make a difference:
First, highlight strengths. Maybe it’s art, sports, storytelling, or problem-solving—whatever it is, make it a point to notice and talk about these talents.
Next, set achievable goals. Breaking big tasks into smaller, manageable steps helps progress feel real and success feel within reach.
Encourage self-advocacy too. It’s about teaching kids—and adults—to speak up about what they need, and to ask for help when they need it.
And don’t forget to model resilience. Let it be known that setbacks are just part of learning. Mistakes? They’re not failures—they’re opportunities to grow.
Here’s a real-world example: maybe a child finds reading tough, but give them a pile of blocks and they can build the most amazing structures, or tell stories that light up a room. When we draw attention to these strengths, it helps them see just how capable and creative they are.
Here’s another idea that really matters: the language we use. Words shape how we see ourselves. Instead of saying “can’t” or “never,” try using “not yet” or “still learning.” It’s a subtle change, but it helps create a mindset where abilities can grow and improve.
A lot of people with dyslexia struggle with negative self-talk—thoughts like “I’m stupid” or “I’ll never get this.” Over time, these thoughts can feel like they’re true. But what if you flipped the script? Practicing positive affirmations and imagining success, even in small ways, can start to change those beliefs and open up new possibilities.
Of course, support from family and teachers is huge, but self-acceptance is just as important. It’s about being proud of your unique way of thinking and seeing yourself as part of a community of creative problem-solvers. Some of the world’s most successful artists and scientists have dyslexia—and their stories prove that different can be a superpower.
So, when we focus on what’s strong, celebrate every bit of effort, and build a nurturing environment, confidence naturally grows. That self-assurance? It becomes the springboard for tackling whatever comes next—and chasing after dreams.
